subject: Biology
title: How Viruses Infect
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: How Viruses Infect.

hook.text: A virus latches onto a cell like a key fitting a lock, using surface proteins to bind receptors.

buildup.text: Once inside, it injects its genetic material and takes over the cell's protein-making machinery.

discovery.text: The cell churns out hundreds of new virus copies until it bursts open, releasing them all.

twist.text: Some viruses hide in your DNA for years—herpes can reactivate decades after the first infection.

climax.text: Each virus targets specific cell types. HIV attacks immune cells. Rabies targets nerve cells.

quiz.question: How do some viruses persist in the body for years?
options: They hide in the host's DNA

details.summary: Viruses infect cells by binding to specific surface receptors, injecting their genetic material, hijacking cellular machinery to replicate, and releasing new viral particles often by destroying the host cell. This cycle of attachment, entry, replication, and release drives viral disease.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding viral infection mechanisms reveals targets for antiviral drugs and vaccines. Each step of the viral life cycle is a potential intervention point.
takeaways: Viruses bind specific host cell receptors determining which cells they can infect
The host cell's own machinery is hijacked to produce viral components
New viruses exit by budding from the cell membrane or by lysing the cell

faq.question: Why can viruses only infect certain types of cells?
faq.answer: Viral surface proteins must match specific receptors on host cells like a key fitting a lock. HIV uses the CD4 receptor found on immune cells. Influenza uses sialic acid receptors in the respiratory tract. This receptor specificity determines viral tropism.

faq.question: How do antiviral drugs work against viral infection?
faq.answer: Antivirals target specific steps in viral replication. Entry inhibitors block receptor binding. Protease inhibitors prevent viral protein processing. Polymerase inhibitors stop viral genome copying. Combination therapy targeting multiple steps prevents resistance.
